case.dispatchHook: St. Petersburg pier. Things moving, nobody admits pushing.
briefing: Agent, reports came in from the St. Petersburg pier. A cart rolled away, a bike did not stop, and a coconut fell.
Every report blames the same thing: something pushed it.
Sort each event by the force behind it, then read the speed logs.
A ghost is not on the list of forces. Check anyway.

lab.intro: Every card is something that moved or stopped moving. Put it with the force that did it.

bins.name: Push or pull
bins.hint: Something touches the object and moves it away or toward itself.

bins.name: Gravity
bins.hint: Earth pulls objects down toward the ground without touching them.

bins.name: Friction
bins.hint: Two surfaces rub together and slow the motion.

bins.name: Magnetic force
bins.hint: A magnet pulls on iron or steel, or pushes or pulls another magnet, without touching.

cards.name: Soccer kick
card: A foot hits a soccer ball.
The ball flies across the field.
cards.why: The foot touches the ball and pushes it away.

cards.name: Wagon of oranges
card: She walks forward and the wagon follows.
cards.why: Holding the handle and drawing the wagon along behind her is a pull.

cards.name: Coconut drop
card: A coconut comes loose from a palm.
Nothing touches it on the way down to the sand.
cards.why: Earth pulls the coconut down to the ground without touching it.

cards.name: Afternoon storm
card: They fall to the street below.
cards.why: Gravity pulls the raindrops down from the cloud to the ground.

cards.name: Bike brakes
card: Rubber pads squeeze the spinning wheel.
cards.why: The pads rub on the wheel and resist its motion, so the bike slows.

cards.name: Book on carpet
card: A book slides across a carpet.
It stops after a short way.
cards.why: The rough carpet rubs on the book and resists its motion.

cards.name: Toy train cars
card: The end of one car comes near the next car.
They snap together before they touch.
cards.why: Magnets on the ends of the cars pull them together without touching.

cards.name: Spilled pins
card: A gray bar is held over steel pins and wooden beads.
The pins jump up to it. The beads stay put.
cards.why: A magnet pulls on steel without touching it, but it does not pull on wood.

case.debriefClosed: Case closed. Every motion on the pier has a force behind it, and none of them are ghosts.
case.debriefOpen: Case stays open for now. The pier logs come back as a cold case soon, and you will read them faster then.

items.stem: An apple breaks off a branch and falls to the ground. A ball thrown straight up slows, stops and comes back down. Which force pulls both objects down?
options: friction
magnetic force
gravity
a push from the air
why: Decoy: friction resists motion when surfaces rub, and it does not pull things down.
Decoy: magnetic force pulls on iron and steel, and apples and balls are not attracted to magnets.
Correct: gravity pulls objects toward Earth without touching them.
Decoy: air pushes back on falling objects a little, which slows them instead of pulling them down.
items.alt: An apple falling from a tree with a downward arrow, and a ball thrown up arcing back down.
items.tisCheck: Gravity acting on falling objects; forces limited to pushes, pulls, friction, gravity and magnetic force.
items.misconceptions: Air thought to push things down; gravity thought to need contact.

items.stem: Four remote-control boats each crossed the same 20 m pool. An agent timed each one. Which boat was the fastest?
options: Boat 1
Boat 2
Boat 3
Boat 4
why: Decoy: Boat 1 took 8 seconds, which is longer than Boat 4's 5 seconds.
Decoy: Boat 2 has the biggest number, 12 seconds, which means it took the longest and was the slowest.
Decoy: Boat 3 took 10 seconds, which is longer than Boat 4's 5 seconds.
Correct: every boat went the same distance, so the boat with the least time, 5 seconds, was the fastest.
items.alt: A table showing four boats that each crossed 20 m: Boat 1 in 8 seconds, Boat 2 in 12 seconds, Boat 3 in 10 seconds and Boat 4 in 5 seconds.
items.tisCheck: Speed as distance in a unit of time (SC.4.P.12.2), read from a table by comparing; no computation.
items.misconceptions: The biggest number in the table taken as the fastest; time and speed confused.

items.stem: The graph shows how far Jo and Sam walked along the St. Petersburg pier over the same amount of time. Jo's line is steeper than Sam's line. Which statement is supported by the graph?
options: Jo walked faster, because Jo covered more distance in the same time.
Sam walked faster, because Sam's line is less steep.
They walked at the same speed, because they walked for the same amount of time.
Jo walked slower, because a steep line means walking uphill.
why: Correct: a steeper line on a distance and time graph means more distance in each unit of time, so Jo was faster.
Decoy: a less steep line means less distance in the same time, so Sam was slower.
Decoy: walking for the same time does not mean walking at the same speed, because Jo went farther.
Decoy: the graph shows distance and time, not hills, so a steep line means fast, not uphill.
items.alt: A distance and time line graph with two lines, a steep line for Jo and a shallow line for Sam.
items.tisCheck: Speed read from a distance and time graph (SC.4.P.12.2); conceptual only, no computation.
items.misconceptions: A graph read as a picture of a hill; the same time taken to mean the same speed.

items.stem: Agents give the same empty cart a light push, a medium push and a hard push on the same smooth floor. They measure how far the cart rolls each time. Which statement is supported by the data?
options: A lighter push makes the cart roll farther.
A harder push makes the cart roll farther.
The cart rolls the same distance no matter how hard the push.
The cart rolls farther because the floor is smooth, not because of the push.
why: Decoy: the light push moved the cart the shortest distance, so this is backward.
Correct: the harder the push, the farther the cart rolled, because a bigger push causes a bigger change in motion.
Decoy: the distances in the table are different for each push.
Decoy: the floor was the same for every push, so the floor cannot explain the different distances.
items.alt: A table showing the cart rolled 1 m after a light push, 3 m after a medium push and 6 m after a hard push.
items.tisCheck: A greater push causes a greater change in motion (SC.5.P.13.2); comparing values only, no computation.
items.misconceptions: The size of a push not linked to motion; a condition held the same (the floor) credited for the change.

items.stem: An agent gives the same toy car the same push on two tracks. The car rolls far on the smooth tile track. It stops much sooner on the carpet track. Why does the car stop sooner on the carpet?
options: The carpet has more friction, which resists the car's motion.
The carpet has less friction, which slows the car down.
Gravity is stronger on the carpet.
The tile track pushes the car forward.
why: Correct: a rough surface like carpet has more friction, and friction resists motion, so the car stops sooner.
Decoy: less friction would let the car roll farther, not stop sooner.
Decoy: gravity pulls the same on both tracks.
Decoy: the tile does not push the car, it just has less friction to slow it.
items.alt: The same toy car on a smooth tile track and on a carpet track, traveling a shorter distance on the carpet.
items.tisCheck: Friction only as resistance to movement; forces limited to pushes, pulls, friction, gravity and magnetic force.
items.misconceptions: Friction thought to push things or to belong to smooth surfaces; gravity thought to change with the surface.

items.stem: An agent holds two bar magnets. When the north pole of one faces the south pole of the other, they pull together. When two north poles face each other, they push apart. What will happen when she turns the magnets so two south poles face each other?
options: They pull together, because all magnet ends attract each other.
Nothing happens, because the magnets are not touching.
They stick together, because magnets attract any metal.
They push apart, because like poles repel.
why: Decoy: the two north poles pushed apart, so magnet ends do not always attract.
Decoy: magnetic force works without touching, as the north poles showed when they pushed apart.
Decoy: magnets attract iron and steel, but two like poles of magnets push apart.
Correct: two south poles are like poles, and like poles repel, just as the two north poles did.
keyWords: north pole of one faces the south pole
two south poles face each other
items.alt: Two bar magnets with north facing south pulling together, and two bar magnets with north facing north pushing apart.
items.tisCheck: Magnetic attraction and repulsion as a force that can act without touching; no field lines.
items.misconceptions: All magnet ends thought to attract; magnetic force thought to need contact.

items.stem: Two teams play tug-of-war on the beach. The table shows how many agents are on each team and how hard each team pulls. Which way will the rope move?
options: toward the right team, because it has more agents
toward the left team, because it pulls harder
nowhere, because both teams are pulling
toward the right team, because the rope moves away from the harder pull
why: Decoy: the number of agents does not decide it, because the left team pulls harder.
Correct: the pulls are not equal, so the rope moves toward the stronger pull.
Decoy: the rope stays still only when both pulls are equal, and these pulls are not.
Decoy: an object moves toward the stronger pull, not away from it.
keyWords: Which way will the rope move
items.alt: A table showing the left team has 4 agents pulling strong and the right team has 5 agents pulling weak.
items.tisCheck: Unequal pulls change an object's motion; described as pulls only, with no term for combined forces.
items.misconceptions: More people thought to always win; any two pulls thought to cancel.

items.stem: Agents tracked a manatee swimming in Tampa Bay. The table shows how far it was from the dock each minute. Which statement describes the manatee's motion?
options: It sped up, because the numbers get bigger each minute.
It slowed down each minute.
It swam the same distance each minute, so its speed stayed the same.
It swam 150 m every minute.
why: Decoy: the numbers grow because the distances add up, but each minute adds the same 50 m, so the manatee did not speed up.
Decoy: each minute adds the same 50 m, so the manatee did not slow down.
Correct: the distance from the dock grew by the same amount each minute, so the manatee kept the same speed.
Decoy: 150 m is how far the manatee was after 3 minutes, not how far it swam in each minute.
keyWords: how far it was from the dock each minute
items.alt: A table showing the manatee was 0 m from the dock at 0 minutes, 50 m at 1 minute, 100 m at 2 minutes and 150 m at 3 minutes.
items.tisCheck: Speed as distance in a unit of time read from a table (SC.4.P.12.2); equal steps of 50 are read as a pattern, no computation is required.
items.misconceptions: Growing totals read as speeding up; total distance mistaken for distance in each minute.

codex.title: Gravity
codex.line: Gravity pulls objects toward Earth, even when nothing touches them.

codex.title: Friction
codex.line: Friction is a force that resists motion when two surfaces rub together.

codex.title: Magnetic force
codex.line: Magnets attract iron and steel, and two like poles of magnets push apart.
